lead: Linux and Windows both store rights on the object, as 6.3 describes. They differ in what sits on the object. Linux puts nine mode bits and a user id on every file. Windows puts a security descriptor holding an access list on every object. Reading both shows how one abstract idea becomes the commands you type. Only a few universities teach this case study.
prereq: You need: rights stored as columns on objects from 6.3, and the idea of a rights ticket from 6.5.

sections.h3: Linux: user ids and mode bits

blocks.text: A Linux process carries a user id (uid) and a group id (gid). Every file records an owner uid, a group gid, and nine permission bits.

The nine bits are read (4), write (2) and execute (1), repeated for owner, group and others. A field's value is the sum: 7 = rwx, 5 = r-x, 4 = r--. The command chmod 754 file sets the three fields to 7, 5 and 4. chown alice file changes the owner. umask is a mask of bits removed when a new file is created: with umask 022 a new file of 666 becomes 644.

Three special bits. setuid makes a program run with the file owner's uid. setgid does the same for the group. The sticky bit on a directory lets a file be deleted or renamed only by the file's owner, the directory's owner or root; /tmp uses this (mode 1777).

POSIX ACLs add per-user entries beyond the nine bits. sudo runs a command as another user after a password check. Linux capabilities split root's power into named units such as CAP_NET_ADMIN. PAM handles authentication. SELinux and AppArmor add mandatory checks that even root cannot skip. Namespaces and cgroups partition and limit processes.

Windows names every user and group by a security identifier (SID), a variable-length number. At login the system builds an access token: the user's SID, the SIDs of the user's groups, and privileges such as SeBackupPrivilege.
Every object has a security descriptor holding two lists. The DACL holds access control entries (ACEs) that allow or deny rights. The SACL records auditing.

The system walks the DACL from the top and stops at the first ACE that matches the token and the requested right. A deny ACE therefore beats any later allow. If no ACE allows the right, access is refused.
UAC (User Account Control) gives an administrator two tokens: a filtered one for normal work and a full one after consent.

spec.aria: Three boxes for the digits 7, 5 and 4 of mode 754, each split into r, w and x bits, with the group box 5 = r-x highlighted and an arrow from bob, a member of group exam, to it.

examples.question: A Linux file has mode 754, owner alice, group exam. User bob is in group exam. (a) Can bob write the file? Can he execute it? (b) A Windows file has this DACL in order: deny bob write, allow exam write, allow alice full control. Bob is in exam. Can bob write?
steps: Split 754: hundreds digit 7 for owner, tens digit 5 for group, units digit 4 for others.
Each digit is a sum of 4 (read), 2 (write), 1 (execute). Owner 7 = 4+2+1 = rwx. Group 5 = 4+1 = r-x. Others 4 = r--.
Bob is not alice, so the owner field is skipped. Bob is in exam, so the group field r-x applies.
r-x gives read = yes, execute = yes, write = no. Bob can execute, cannot write.
Windows: the first ACE matching bob's write request is the deny entry. Evaluation stops there, so bob is denied.
Removing the deny entry leaves allow exam write as the first match, and bob can write.
examples.answer: Bob cannot write the Linux file but can execute it (group field 5 = r-x); on Windows the deny ACE is reached first, so he cannot write until that entry is removed.
examples.check:
mode = 754
owner = mode // 100
group = (mode // 10) % 10
others = mode % 10
print(owner, group, others)
print(1 if group & 2 else 0, 1 if group & 1 else 0)

traps: Reading 754 as three unrelated digits instead of 4-2-1 sums.
Forgetting that a process holding the file's uid skips the group and other fields entirely.
In Windows, forgetting that the DACL is read top to bottom and the first matching ACE decides: a deny ACE beats an allow only because deny ACEs are normally stored first in the list.
Mixing up setuid (run as file owner) with sudo (run as a chosen user after a password).
Reading mode bits as if they applied in order like a DACL; Linux picks one field, owner first, then group, then others.

quiz.q: What does uid 0 mean in Linux?
quiz.a: Root, the superuser; it bypasses the ordinary permission checks.

quiz.q: Why does the digit 5 mean r-x?
quiz.a: 5 = 4 + 1, read plus execute. The write bit 2 is absent.

quiz.q: umask is 022 and a program creates a file with requested mode 666. What mode results?
quiz.a: 666 AND NOT 022: write bits for group and others are cleared, giving 644 = rw-r--r--.

quiz.q: Name the two lists inside a Windows security descriptor.
quiz.a: The DACL (allows and denies) and the SACL (auditing).

quiz.q: A file has mode 640. What can a group member do?
quiz.a: Group digit 4 = r--. The member can read only; write and execute are refused.

quiz.q: A DACL lists allow exam full control, then deny bob write. Bob is in exam. Can bob write?
quiz.a: Yes. The first matching ACE is allow exam full control: exam is in bob's token and that ACE covers write, so checking stops and write is granted. He would be denied only if the deny ACE came before the allow, for example deny bob write placed first.

beyond: Not for the exam. Both designs are converging: Linux gained POSIX ACLs and capabilities, and Windows gained AppContainer sandboxes. Modern container isolation borrows Linux namespaces and cgroups, while Windows uses job objects and silos. Search 'Linux capabilities man page', 'Windows access check' and 'SELinux type enforcement' to go further.
